newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-WORLD SERIES OPENER WASHED OUT, MANAGERS ADJUST.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-WORLD SERIES OPENER WASHED OUT, MANAGERS ADJUST.

text.p: Heavy rain and wind capsized Game 1 of the World Series Saturday, rearranged the Atlanta Braves' pitching rotation and threatened to wash out Sunday's rescheduled opener against the New York Yankees.

With at least one extra day off after clinching the National League pennant Thursday, Braves manager Bobby Cox moved four-time Cy Young award winner Greg Maddux up to the number two spot in the rotation behind Game 1 starter John Smoltz, this year's probable N.L. Cy Young winner.
Denny Neagle was dropped to the four slot behind another Cy Young winner, Tom Glavine.

On the Yankees' side, manager Joe Torre said left-hander Kenny Rogers will pitch Game 4. "No one else was considered," he said. "Playing the Braves, it's going to be the left-handed starter," said Torre in view of the left-handed batting prowess of the defending World Series champions.

Previously, with Monday's scheduled but now vanished off-day, there had been the chance of Torre's Game 1 starter Andy Pettitte, the likely American League Cy Young winner, returning for Game 4 on three days' rest.
Pettitte and Game 2 starter Jimmy Key are lefties, while Game 3 pick David Cone is Torre's only right-hander.

Rogers has struggled in the post-season. Starting two games and relieving in another, he pitched to a terrifying 10.30 earned run average, lasting just five innings and giving up 10 hits and six runs. But Torre defended him.
"Every time I send Kenny out there, even though it hasn't worked in the post-season, I still believe he's going to get us the five or six innings that would help us win a ball game," said Torre.

The pitching-rich Braves would seem to have an advantage if Sunday were also washed out and the two teams had to play seven in a row, possibly needing five starters. "It would not be a major problem," said Cox, naming Steve Avery and Mike Bielecki as his first two options.
Torre did not address the question.
The weather forecast for Sunday was not hopeful.

"When it starts we'll be ready," said Torre. "Hopefully the weather will cooperate somewhat. It's a mess out there now and from what we've heard it may continue into tomorrow which means the field is going to be wet. I don't think that's an advantage for either team."
But he did say Darryl Strawberry, who has a small fracture in his right foot, might benefit from Saturday's rainout.

"I'm not sure Darryl could have played today even if it was dry, only because he wasn't as good yesterday moving around as he was the day before. But who knows, the day off may benefit him and he'll be able to play."
Torre's other left-fielder, Tim Raines, could also have trouble with poor footing at Yankee Stadium because of a longstanding hamstring problem. Right-fielder Paul O'Neill also has hamstring woes.

Cox said he would use left-handed slugger Ryan Klesko as the designated hitter against Pettitte in the American League park, where the infield was covered with tarpaulins but the outfield was inundated Saturday.

Right field was under standing pools of water, with the top surface washed away so that old football stripes showed through every five yards. The water was more than one inch (2 cm) deep between the right foul line and the fence. In left field, there was a big puddle behind shortstop.
In the stands, water cascaded down from the upper decks and streams ran down the aisles. A waterfall some 10 feet (3 metres) wide poured down from the left-field upper deck.
Despite the miserable conditions, some fans stood outside the stadium trying to buy tickets.
"I'm stupid, the game is called, and supposedly, hopefully, tickets will go on sale," one fan explained.

Some would-be buyers noted that tickets -- which scalpers have sold for hundreds and even thousands of dollars -- might become available from people unable to change their plans to adjust to the new schedule of games.
